concepts.title: CloudWatch: Metrics, Logs, and Alarms
concepts.description: CloudWatch is AWS's built-in observability service -- metrics tell you what's happening in aggregate, logs tell you what happened in detail, and alarms turn either into an automated reaction; treating them as one undifferentiated 'monitoring' blob is how teams end up flying blind or drowning in noise.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a CloudWatch metric and a CloudWatch log, and when each is the right tool to reach for.
Describe how metrics are structured (namespace, dimensions, statistic, period) and how that structure enables aggregation and filtering.
Explain the difference between AWS-published metrics (e.g. EC2 CPUUtilization) and custom/agent-collected metrics (e.g. memory usage), and why some 'obvious' metrics require an agent.
Read a Logs Insights query well enough to explain what it computes from raw log lines.
Explain how an alarm's period, evaluation periods, and datapoints-to-alarm settings interact to decide when it actually fires.
Explain why Average is often the wrong statistic for latency, and when a percentile statistic is the better choice.

sections.heading: Metrics: Numbers Sampled Over Time
sections.body:
A CloudWatch **metric** is a time-ordered series of data points for something you (or AWS) chose to measure -- CPUUtilization, RequestCount, ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, and thousands of others. Every metric lives inside a **namespace** (a rough grouping, like `AWS/EC2` or `AWS/RDS`, that keeps different services' metrics from colliding), and is further identified by a set of **dimensions** -- key/value pairs like `InstanceId=i-0abc123` that let CloudWatch distinguish 'CPUUtilization for this specific instance' from 'CPUUtilization for that other instance,' even though both metrics share the same name and namespace. When you graph or alarm on a metric, you're really querying a specific namespace + metric name + dimension combination, aggregated over a chosen **period** (the time bucket -- 1 minute, 5 minutes, 1 hour) using a chosen **statistic** (Average, Sum, Maximum, Minimum, or a percentile like p99).

Most AWS services publish a baseline set of metrics automatically, at no extra effort on your part -- EC2 publishes CPUUtilization, NetworkIn/Out, and disk I/O counters every 5 minutes by default (1 minute if you enable detailed monitoring, at a small additional cost). But there's a specific, very common surprise here: **EC2 does not publish memory utilization, disk space used, or any metric that requires looking inside the guest operating system**, because the hypervisor genuinely cannot see inside the instance's OS -- only the instance's own OS can observe how much of its RAM is actually in use. Getting that data into CloudWatch requires installing the **CloudWatch agent** on the instance itself, which then pushes those OS-level readings up as custom metrics. This trips up almost everyone the first time they go looking for a memory graph on a freshly launched EC2 instance and find nothing there at all -- not a flat line at zero, an absent metric entirely, because nothing has ever published it.

sections.heading: Logs: What Actually Happened, Not Just the Aggregate
sections.body:
Where metrics answer 'how much / how many, over time,' **CloudWatch Logs** answers 'what exactly happened, in what order, with what detail.' Applications and services write log lines into a **log group** (a named container, typically one per application or per Lambda function), and within a log group, a **log stream** represents one particular source of those lines -- one EC2 instance, one Lambda invocation environment, one ECS task. Log data arrives as raw text (or structured JSON, if your application logs that way), and unlike a metric, it isn't pre-aggregated into a number -- you query it after the fact using **CloudWatch Logs Insights**, a purpose-built query language that looks a little like SQL crossed with a Unix pipeline:

```text
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count(*) as errorCount by bin(5m)
| sort errorCount desc
```

This query scans a log group's raw lines, keeps only ones containing `ERROR`, buckets them into 5-minute windows, counts each bucket, and sorts by count -- effectively turning unstructured text into the kind of time-series view a metric would have given natively, but computed on demand from the raw log content rather than pre-aggregated as the data arrived.

A detail that catches people off guard specifically because it's a genuine cost trap, not just a mild inconvenience: **log groups default to Never Expire retention**. Every line an application writes accumulates in that log group forever, at CloudWatch Logs' per-GB storage price, until someone explicitly sets a retention period (1 week, 1 month, 1 year, and various options between). A chatty application logging at DEBUG level in production, left on the default retention setting for a year, can quietly become a genuinely significant and completely avoidable line item on the monthly bill -- the fix is simply to set an explicit retention policy on every log group at creation time, matched to how long that group's data is actually useful for debugging or compliance, rather than leaving it on the default and forgetting about it.

sections.heading: Alarms: Turning a Metric Into an Automatic Reaction
sections.body:
A CloudWatch **alarm** watches a single metric (or a math expression combining several) and transitions between three states: **OK** (the metric is behaving), **ALARM** (it has breached the configured threshold), and **INSUFFICIENT_DATA** (CloudWatch doesn't yet have enough recent datapoints to evaluate the alarm at all -- a distinct, calmer state from ALARM, common right after an alarm is first created or after a resource stops reporting a metric entirely, such as a terminated instance).

An alarm's actual firing behavior is governed by three settings working together, and getting this combination wrong is one of the most common sources of both false alarms and missed real ones: **period** (the size of each evaluation bucket -- e.g. 60 seconds), **evaluation periods** (how many of the most recent buckets to look at -- e.g. 5), and **datapoints to alarm** (how many of those evaluated buckets actually need to breach the threshold to trigger ALARM -- e.g. 3 out of 5). Setting evaluation periods and datapoints to alarm equal to each other (e.g. 5 of 5) makes the alarm strict and slow to fire, requiring a sustained breach across the entire window -- good for avoiding noise from a single transient spike, but slower to notify you of a real, ongoing problem. Setting datapoints to alarm lower than evaluation periods (e.g. 3 of 5) makes the alarm sensitive to an intermittent, flapping condition without demanding a continuous breach for the whole window, which is often the better match for real-world noisy metrics that briefly dip in and out of a bad state.

An alarm can also be configured for how it treats missing data specifically (`missing`, `notBreaching`, `breaching`, or `ignore`) -- this matters a lot for something like a health-check metric that a dead or terminated instance simply stops reporting altogether: if missing data is treated as `notBreaching` (a common default), an instance that goes completely dark -- the worst possible outcome -- can paradoxically leave the alarm sitting calmly in OK or INSUFFICIENT_DATA instead of firing, precisely because there's no data at all to evaluate as a breach. This is a subtle trap worth checking explicitly for any alarm meant to catch total failure, not just degraded performance.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes: The Wrong Statistic, and Averages That Hide Problems
sections.body:
Choosing **Average** as the default statistic for almost everything is a natural habit, and it's frequently the wrong choice for exactly the metrics people care about most -- request latency being the classic example. If 99 requests out of 100 complete in 50ms and one takes 5 seconds, the Average across that batch looks like a perfectly reasonable ~99ms -- comfortably hiding the one request that a real user actually experienced as a 5-second hang. Percentile statistics (p90, p99, p99.9) are specifically designed to surface exactly this kind of tail behavior: p99 answers 'what's the worst experience the slowest 1% of requests actually had,' a materially different, and usually far more actionable, question than 'what's the mean.' The practical rule of thumb: use Average or Sum for capacity-style metrics where the aggregate genuinely is what matters (total bytes transferred, total request count), and reach for a percentile statistic -- almost always p99 or higher -- for anything latency-related, where a small fraction of genuinely bad outcomes is precisely the thing you're trying to catch and an average will systematically wash it out.

A second, related mistake is sizing the alarm's period too coarsely for the thing being measured -- a 1-hour period on a metric that spikes for 10 minutes at a time will often average that spike down below the threshold entirely, never firing at all, even though real users experienced a real problem for those 10 minutes. Matching the period to how quickly the underlying condition can meaningfully change, and reaching for a percentile statistic rather than a mean whenever tail behavior matters, are both about the same underlying discipline: making sure the number the alarm actually evaluates still resembles the thing you were trying to detect in the first place, rather than an aggregation that happens to erase it.

examples.title: A CloudWatch Logs Insights Query for Error-Rate Spikes
examples.code:
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter @message like /ERROR/
| stats count(*) as errorCount by bin(5m)
| sort errorCount desc
| limit 20
examples.explanation: This query scans a log group's raw lines rather than reading a pre-aggregated number the way a metric graph would. `filter @message like /ERROR/` discards every line that doesn't contain the literal text `ERROR`, `stats count(*) as errorCount by bin(5m)` groups the surviving lines into 5-minute buckets and counts how many fall in each one, and `sort errorCount desc` puts the noisiest windows first so you can jump straight to the worst period rather than scrolling a raw log chronologically. This is exactly the kind of question logs answer that metrics can't on their own: a metric could tell you an error-rate alarm fired, but Logs Insights is what lets you go from 'something was wrong around 2:15pm' to 'here are the 40 error lines from that specific five-minute window' in one query, computed on demand rather than requiring the error rate to have been pre-published as a metric in advance.

examples.title: Alarming on p99 Latency Instead of Average
examples.explanation: `--extended-statistic "p99"` (rather than `--statistic Average`) means this alarm evaluates the response time experienced by the slowest 1% of requests in each period, not the mean across all of them -- exactly the choice that keeps a rare-but-real tail-latency problem from being averaged away into invisibility. `--period 60` with `--evaluation-periods 5` and `--datapoints-to-alarm 3` means the alarm looks at the most recent five 60-second buckets and fires once at least three of them show p99 above the 1.0 second threshold -- sensitive enough to catch a real, ongoing problem within a few minutes without firing off a single noisy 60-second blip. `--treat-missing-data notBreaching` means if the load balancer temporarily stops reporting this metric, the alarm won't treat that silence as a breach on its own (a reasonable choice here, though worth re-examining for any alarm meant specifically to catch total outages rather than degraded latency).

examples.title: Publishing a Custom Application Metric CloudWatch Doesn't Know About
examples.explanation: AWS-published metrics only cover what AWS's own services already know about internally -- nothing in EC2 or CloudWatch has any way of knowing how many jobs are sitting in an application-defined queue, because that number only exists inside the application's own logic. `put_metric_data` is how any application pushes an arbitrary number, under a namespace it chooses (`MyApp/Queues` here, kept distinct from any AWS namespace), into CloudWatch as a first-class custom metric -- once published, it can be graphed and alarmed on exactly like `CPUUtilization`, with the same statistics, periods, and alarm machinery. This is the general escape hatch for 'CloudWatch doesn't have a metric for the thing I actually care about': if AWS didn't publish it, and it matters, publish it yourself. It's worth knowing custom metrics are billed per metric per month, so this is a deliberate choice for genuinely important signals, not something to do reflexively for every internal counter.

misconceptions.description: If CloudWatch isn't showing a metric like memory utilization for my EC2 instance, that must mean memory usage is fine.
misconceptions.clarification: EC2 does not publish memory, disk space, or any other guest-OS-level metric by default, because the hypervisor has no visibility inside the instance's operating system -- only the OS itself can observe that. An absent metric means nothing has ever been configured to collect and publish it (typically via the CloudWatch agent), not that the underlying value is healthy. A missing graph is a monitoring gap, not a clean bill of health.

misconceptions.description: An alarm in state INSUFFICIENT_DATA means something is broken and needs immediate attention, the same as ALARM.
misconceptions.clarification: INSUFFICIENT_DATA specifically means CloudWatch doesn't have enough recent datapoints to evaluate the alarm at all -- common right after an alarm is first created, or when a resource has stopped reporting a metric entirely (for example, because it was terminated on purpose). It is a distinct state from ALARM, which means the metric was actually evaluated and found to be breaching the threshold. Treating the two identically either causes unnecessary panic over routine situations (a brand-new alarm with no history yet) or, worse, trains people to ignore INSUFFICIENT_DATA notifications that occasionally do indicate a real problem, like an instance that silently stopped reporting because it crashed.

exercises.prompt: Given this alarm configuration and CPU utilization timeline, determine exactly which minute the alarm first transitions from OK to ALARM, and explain why.
exercises.code:
alarm config: period=60s, evaluation_periods=5, datapoints_to_alarm=3, threshold=80 (GreaterThanThreshold), statistic=Average

minute  CPUUtilization
1       55
2       82   (breach)
3       60
4       85   (breach)
5       88   (breach)
6       90   (breach)
hints: The alarm doesn't require 5 CONSECUTIVE breaching minutes -- it requires 3 breaching datapoints among the most recent 5 evaluated periods.
At each minute, ask: looking back across the most recent 5 one-minute periods (or fewer, if the alarm hasn't existed that long), how many of them breached 80?
Count breaches within the rolling 5-minute window ending at minute 5, not the whole timeline at once.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The alarm fires at minute 5. Looking at the rolling window of the 5 most recent periods (minutes 1-5), there are breaches at minutes 2, 4, and 5 -- exactly 3 breaching datapoints, which meets datapoints_to_alarm=3, so the alarm transitions to ALARM at minute 5, not earlier (only 2 breaches existed by minute 4) and not minute 6 (it had already fired by then).
exercises.solutionExplanation: datapoints_to_alarm=3 out of evaluation_periods=5 means CloudWatch evaluates a sliding window of the 5 most recent periods and checks whether at least 3 of them breached the threshold -- it does not require those 3 to be consecutive. By minute 4, the window covering minutes 1-4 (fewer than 5 periods exist yet, but CloudWatch evaluates what's available) contains breaches at minutes 2 and 4 -- only 2, not enough. By minute 5, the window of minutes 1-5 contains breaches at 2, 4, and 5 -- exactly 3, crossing the threshold, so the alarm fires at minute 5. Minute 6's breach is irrelevant to when the alarm first fired, since the transition to ALARM already happened one minute earlier.

exercises.prompt: A metric filter is supposed to count how many log lines represent a failed payment, but it never matches anything, even though the application logs failures constantly. Find and fix the bug.
hints: A CloudWatch Logs metric filter pattern with space-separated terms requires each literal term to actually appear in the log line -- check whether every term in the pattern is actually present.
Look closely at the log level the application actually logs failed payments at, versus the level the pattern requires.
The goal is to match lines representing a failed payment -- does the pattern need to depend on a specific log level term at all to achieve that?
exercises.solutionCode:
// Fixed metric filter pattern -- matches on the term that's actually guaranteed present
"payment_failed"
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original pattern `"ERROR payment_failed"` requires both literal terms to be present in a log line for it to match. The application actually logs failed payments at `[WARN]`, not `[ERROR]` -- so the literal term `ERROR` never appears in any of these lines, and the filter matches zero lines despite failures happening constantly. The fix drops the dependency on a log-level term that doesn't reflect reality and matches on `payment_failed` alone, which is the term that's actually guaranteed to be present whenever this specific failure occurs. A more general lesson: metric filter patterns match literal text, not intent -- it's worth checking an actual sample log line, not just the code that appears to produce it, before trusting a pattern's assumptions about level or wording.

assessments.prompt: An API's average response time looks healthy at 120ms, but a growing number of user complaints describe multi-second hangs. Which change to the monitoring setup is most likely to actually surface this problem?
options: Lower the alarm threshold on the existing Average-based latency alarm.
Switch the alarm's statistic from Average to a high percentile like p99, since a small fraction of very slow requests can be averaged away into an unremarkable mean.
Increase the alarm's period from 60 seconds to 1 hour so it has more data to average over.
Switch the metric's namespace to a custom namespace so it can be graphed separately.
assessments.explanation: A small number of genuinely slow requests mixed into a much larger number of fast ones is exactly the scenario Average is bad at surfacing -- the mean gets pulled only slightly by a handful of outliers, while a percentile statistic like p99 specifically reports what the slowest fraction of requests actually experienced. Lowering the threshold on an Average-based alarm (option A) doesn't fix the underlying blind spot; the average was never going to spike enough to cross a reasonable threshold in the first place. Increasing the period (option C) makes the problem worse, not better, by averaging over an even larger, more diluting window. Changing the namespace (option D) is purely organizational and has no effect on which statistic is being evaluated.

assessments.prompt: Explain how an alarm's period, evaluation periods, and datapoints-to-alarm settings interact, and why misconfiguring them can cause both false positives (noisy pages for transient blips) and false negatives (missing a real, ongoing problem).
assessments.modelAnswer: An alarm's period defines the size of each individual bucket of aggregated metric data -- say, 60 seconds. Evaluation periods defines how many of the most recent buckets CloudWatch looks at when deciding whether to fire -- say, 5, meaning the most recent 5 minutes of buckets at a 60-second period. Datapoints to alarm defines how many of those evaluated buckets actually need to have breached the threshold for the alarm to transition to ALARM -- say, 3. These three settings interact as a sliding window with a threshold count, not a simple 'is the metric currently over X' check: CloudWatch keeps re-evaluating the most recent N buckets (N = evaluation periods) on every new datapoint, and fires the moment at least M of those N buckets (M = datapoints to alarm) have breached. Setting M equal to N (say, 5 of 5) makes the alarm demand a sustained breach across the entire window before firing at all -- this avoids false positives from a single transient spike, since one bad minute out of five won't be enough, but it's slower to notify anyone of a genuinely ongoing problem, since every one of those five buckets has to be bad. Setting M below N (say, 3 of 5) makes the alarm considerably more sensitive to an intermittent, flapping condition, firing even if the metric dips in and out of breach rather than staying pinned above the threshold continuously -- which is often a better match for real, noisy production metrics, but it can also mean a handful of genuinely unrelated transient spikes scattered across the window trigger a page even though nothing is continuously wrong. Getting this wrong in either direction has a real cost: too strict (M close to N, or a coarse period that averages spikes away) produces false negatives, silently missing real problems that don't happen to be perfectly sustained for the whole window; too loose (M much smaller than N, or a very short period reacting to normal noise) produces false positives, paging on transient blips that resolve on their own and eventually teaching whoever's on call to stop trusting or promptly responding to alerts from this alarm at all.

concepts.title: Alerting Without Alert Fatigue
concepts.description: A monitoring system that pages a human for everything eventually trains that human to ignore it entirely; designing alerts around what genuinely requires action -- not just what CloudWatch is capable of measuring -- is what keeps an on-call rotation actually responsive when something real breaks.
learningObjectives: Explain why alert fatigue is a predictable, structural consequence of paging on every anomaly rather than every actionable condition.

Distinguish symptom-based alerting (user-facing impact) from cause-based alerting (internal metric anomalies), and explain why symptom-based alerts should page while cause-based signals usually shouldn't.
Design a basic alert severity tiering scheme (page vs ticket vs dashboard-only) and match each tier to an appropriate notification channel.
Explain how composite alarms and anomaly detection reduce noisy single-metric alarms into fewer, more meaningful signals.
Explain why an alert's content -- not just its existence -- affects how quickly a real incident gets resolved.

sections.heading: Alert Fatigue Is a Predictable, Structural Failure Mode
sections.body: It feels intuitively safer to alarm on everything CloudWatch is capable of measuring -- more coverage sounds like it can only help. In practice, this reliably backfires, and not because of carelessness: it's a direct, predictable consequence of how humans respond to a high volume of low-value interruptions. If an on-call engineer receives a dozen pages a week for conditions that turn out to be harmless -- a CPU blip during a known nightly batch job, a metric that briefly crossed a threshold and immediately recovered on its own -- they don't (and realistically can't) treat every one of those with full urgency indefinitely. They start habituating: glancing at a page, recognizing the familiar 'oh, that one again' pattern, and dismissing it without fully investigating. The problem is that this habituation doesn't selectively apply to the noisy alarms -- it dulls the response to *all* pages from that same channel, including the rare one that's actually a real, novel incident. The fix isn't 'be more disciplined about checking every page carefully' -- that's fighting basic human attention economics. The fix is to stop sending pages that don't warrant full urgency in the first place, so that a page reliably means something when it does arrive.

sections.heading: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alerting
sections.body:
A useful, concrete distinction: a **symptom-based** alert fires on something a user (or the business) would actually notice or be harmed by -- an elevated 5xx error rate on a customer-facing endpoint, checkout latency crossing a threshold that meaningfully affects conversion, an availability drop on the login flow. A **cause-based** alert fires on an internal condition that might, or might not, be contributing to a symptom -- CPU utilization at 85%, memory climbing, a queue depth trending upward. The relationship between them matters: a cause-based signal can be perfectly correct and still not warrant paging anyone, because plenty of causes never actually produce a user-visible symptom (a batch job legitimately pegs CPU at 85% every night at 2am with zero customer impact), and because a real symptom can have causes nobody predicted or instrumented in advance.

The practical rule this suggests: reserve paging -- something that interrupts a person, day or night, and demands action within minutes -- for symptom-based conditions that are close to actual user or business impact. Cause-based metrics remain genuinely valuable, just not as page triggers on their own -- they belong on dashboards, in lower-urgency tickets, or as supporting context that someone already responding to a symptom-based page pulls up to start diagnosing *why* the symptom is happening. This is exactly the same underlying discipline as choosing p99 over Average in the previous concept: matching the signal you actually act on to the thing you actually care about, rather than the thing that happened to be easiest to measure.

sections.heading: Tiering Severity and Routing Alerts Appropriately
sections.body:
A workable alerting scheme typically has at least three tiers, each with a genuinely different notification channel and expected response time, rather than routing everything to the same pager: **Page** (routed to an on-call rotation via something like PagerDuty or an SNS topic wired to a paging integration, expected to be acknowledged and acted on within minutes, reserved for symptom-based, user-impacting conditions), **Ticket** (creates a tracked work item for business-hours follow-up -- appropriate for a cause-based trend worth investigating soon but not urgently, like disk usage climbing toward a limit weeks out), and **Dashboard-only / informational** (visible when someone looks, never actively pushed to anyone -- appropriate for routine operational metrics that are useful context but don't represent an anomaly on their own).

A closely related technique for reducing noise without reducing coverage is the **composite alarm**: rather than three separate alarms independently paging for elevated error rate, elevated latency, and a drop in healthy host count -- three pages for what's very likely the same underlying event -- a composite alarm combines several underlying alarm states with AND/OR logic and only enters ALARM (and only then triggers the page) when the combination genuinely indicates a real incident, such as elevated errors *and* a drop in healthy hosts together. This directly reduces the page count for a single incident from three to one, without silencing or deleting any of the underlying signals, which remain available individually on a dashboard for diagnosis.

sections.heading: Runbooks and Actionable Alert Content
sections.body:
An alert's *existence* is only half of what makes it useful -- its *content* determines how quickly whoever receives it can actually do something about it. A page that says only 'ALARM: HighErrorRate' forces the person paged to reconstruct context from scratch at 3am: which service, which dashboard to open, what's the normal baseline, has this happened before, what's the first thing to check. A well-designed alert includes, or links directly to, the specific dashboard for the affected service, the relevant runbook (a short, maintained document describing the first few diagnostic steps and known common causes for this specific alarm), and enough detail in the alert text itself (which metric, which threshold, current value) that the responder doesn't have to go looking for the basics before they can even start investigating.

This matters more than it might seem, because the cost of a page isn't just whether it fires appropriately -- it's also how long it takes the person who receives it to go from 'woken up by a notification' to 'actually diagnosing the right thing.' An alert that anticipates and shortens that gap, even for a genuinely rare, real incident, materially improves how fast the team actually responds -- which is the entire point of paging in the first place.

examples.title: A Composite Alarm Turning Three Flapping Alarms Into One Meaningful Page
examples.explanation: Instead of two independent alarms -- one on elevated 5xx rate, one on a drop in healthy target-group hosts -- each separately configured to page, this composite alarm only enters ALARM when *both* underlying alarms are simultaneously in ALARM. A brief 5xx blip with hosts otherwise healthy (often a transient, self-recovering condition) no longer pages on its own, and neither does a healthy-host dip caused by a routine deploy cycling instances in and out. The combination of both conditions together is a much stronger signal of a real, ongoing outage than either alone, and it produces exactly one page for that one real incident, rather than two separate, individually-noisier alarms both firing and re-firing throughout the same event.

examples.title: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alarm Configuration, Side by Side
examples.code:
# Symptom-based: pages, because it's close to real user impact
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "checkout-5xx-rate-high" \
  --namespace "AWS/ApplicationELB" --metric-name "HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count" \
  --statistic Sum --period 60 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 \
  --threshold 10 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:oncall-alerts

# Cause-based: dashboard-only, no paging action attached
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "checkout-instance-cpu-elevated" \
  --namespace "AWS/EC2" --metric-name "CPUUtilization" \
  --dimensions Name=AutoScalingGroupName,Value=checkout-asg \
  --statistic Average --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 3 \
  --threshold 75 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold
examples.explanation: Both alarms are entirely valid and worth having, but they serve different purposes and are configured accordingly. The first watches 5xx error count on the customer-facing checkout endpoint -- a direct symptom of real user impact -- and has `--alarm-actions` pointed at the on-call SNS topic, so it pages. The second watches EC2 CPU on the same service's instances -- a possible cause, but not itself a guarantee of any user-visible problem, since the autoscaling group might simply be handling normal elevated load just fine -- and deliberately has no `--alarm-actions` at all, meaning it will still transition between OK and ALARM and be fully visible on a CloudWatch dashboard, but it will never interrupt anyone. If checkout error rates do spike later, this CPU alarm's history is exactly the kind of cause-based context someone would pull up while investigating the page that the first alarm triggered.

examples.title: Anomaly Detection Instead of a Static Threshold for a Seasonal Metric
examples.code:
aws cloudwatch put-anomaly-detector \
  --namespace "AWS/ApplicationELB" --metric-name "RequestCount" \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/my-alb/1234567890abcdef \
  --stat Average

aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "request-count-anomalous" \
  --namespace "AWS/ApplicationELB" --metric-name "RequestCount" \
  --dimensions Name=LoadBalancer,Value=app/my-alb/1234567890abcdef \
  --statistic Average --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 --datapoints-to-alarm 2 \
  --comparison-operator LessThanLowerOrGreaterThanUpperThreshold \
  --threshold-metric-id ad1 \
  --metrics 'file://anomaly-metric-math.json' \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:oncall-alerts
examples.explanation: Traffic to a typical web service is rarely flat -- it's higher during business hours and on weekdays, lower overnight and on weekends, and any single static threshold has to choose between two bad options: set low enough to catch a real overnight traffic drop (a possible outage signal), it fires every single night as expected low-traffic hours begin; set high enough to survive the normal overnight dip without firing, it becomes too loose to reliably catch a real drop during business hours, when the same absolute request count would actually be alarming. CloudWatch's anomaly detection models the metric's normal range as a learned band that itself varies by time of day and day of week, and this alarm fires only when the actual value falls outside that expected band -- so a normal 2am traffic dip stays inside the (correspondingly lower) expected band and never fires, while a real, anomalous drop or spike at any hour, business hours included, does. This directly solves the false-positive-vs-false-negative trade a static 3am-safe threshold could never fully escape.

misconceptions.description: The safest alerting strategy is to alarm on every metric available, since more monitoring coverage can only help.
misconceptions.clarification: Paging on every available signal degrades the signal-to-noise ratio of the paging channel itself, to the point where a real, urgent page gets the same dulled, delayed response as routine noise -- a well-documented human attention effect, not a discipline failure on the responder's part. The fix isn't less monitoring coverage; it's routing most of that coverage to dashboards and tickets rather than pages, reserving paging specifically for symptom-based, user-impacting conditions.

misconceptions.description: A static-threshold alarm and an anomaly-detection alarm are basically interchangeable ways to alert on the same metric.
misconceptions.clarification: A static threshold doesn't account for a metric's expected variation over time (daily or weekly seasonality) -- it's either set loose enough to survive normal peaks and troughs, in which case it misses real problems that occur during a normally-quiet period, or tight enough to catch real problems, in which case it fires constantly during entirely normal peaks or troughs. Anomaly detection instead models the expected band of normal values (which itself moves with time-of-day and day-of-week patterns) and alerts on deviation from that band, which is a genuinely different mechanism suited to seasonal metrics that a single fixed number cannot represent well.

exercises.prompt: An on-call engineer has started silencing pages from their phone overnight because they're paged roughly 30 times a week, and nearly all of those pages turn out to be a CPUUtilization alarm firing every night during a known, harmless data-warehouse batch job. Diagnose the design problem with this alerting setup and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
alarm: nightly-batch-cpu-high
metric: AWS/EC2 CPUUtilization, AutoScalingGroupName=batch-asg
threshold: > 70% average, period=300s, evaluation_periods=3, datapoints_to_alarm=3
action: pages on-call via SNS -> PagerDuty, every single night around 1am
hints: Ask whether this alarm is symptom-based (something a user would notice) or cause-based (an internal condition that may or may not matter) -- and what that implies about whether it should page at all.
The batch job's CPU usage being high every night is described as expected and harmless -- does an expected, harmless condition need to interrupt a human in real time?

Consider what should actually page here instead: is there a more direct signal of the batch job genuinely failing or overrunning, rather than a proxy metric (CPU) that happens to correlate with it running normally?
exercises.solutionCode:
# Remove the paging action from the CPU alarm entirely -- keep it as a dashboard-only signal
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name nightly-batch-cpu-high ... # (no --alarm-actions)

# Add a symptom-based alarm on the actual thing that matters: did the batch job fail or run too long
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "nightly-batch-job-failed-or-overran" \
  --namespace "MyApp/BatchJobs" --metric-name "JobDurationMinutes" \
  --statistic Maximum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 --datapoints-to-alarm 1 \
  --threshold 120 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --treat-missing-data breaching \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:oncall-alerts
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original alarm is a cause-based signal (elevated CPU) being used as if it were a symptom-based one (something actually wrong), when in reality high CPU during this specific job is entirely expected and never itself indicates a problem -- it fires reliably every night purely because the job runs successfully, which is exactly the pattern that produces the habituation and eventual silencing described in the scenario. The fix removes the paging action from the CPU alarm (it can remain as a dashboard signal, useful context if something else does go wrong) and replaces the page trigger with a genuinely symptom-based signal: a custom metric the batch job itself publishes reporting its own duration, alarmed on directly exceeding an expected runtime, with `--treat-missing-data breaching` so that the job never even reporting a completion time at all (e.g. because it crashed outright) is treated as exactly the kind of failure that should page, rather than being silently ignored as merely 'no data.'

exercises.prompt: Write a CloudWatch composite alarm (as an AWS CLI command) that pages only when BOTH an elevated 5xx error rate alarm ('api-5xx-high') AND a low healthy-host-count alarm ('api-healthy-hosts-low') are simultaneously in ALARM, instead of paging separately for each.
hints: The --alarm-rule expression uses ALARM("alarm-name") as a boolean building block, combined with AND/OR/NOT.
The composite alarm itself needs its own --alarm-actions pointed at the SNS topic -- the underlying two alarms don't need paging actions of their own if only the composite should page.
Give the composite alarm a name that describes the combined condition, distinct from either underlying alarm's name.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The `--alarm-rule` expression `ALARM("api-5xx-high") AND ALARM("api-healthy-hosts-low")` means this composite alarm only enters its own ALARM state when both underlying, independently-evaluated alarms are simultaneously in ALARM -- either one alone (a brief error blip with hosts otherwise healthy, or a host-count dip during a routine deploy with error rates unaffected) is not enough to trigger it. Only the composite alarm carries `--alarm-actions`, so the two underlying alarms remain fully visible and independently trackable (useful for diagnosis) but no longer independently page anyone -- collapsing what would have been up to two separate pages for the same real incident into exactly one, without losing any of the underlying signal.

assessments.prompt: A team is deciding which of two conditions should page an on-call engineer: (1) checkout page error rate exceeding 2% for 3 minutes, or (2) database CPU utilization exceeding 60%. Which is the better candidate for paging, and why?
options: Database CPU exceeding 60%, because catching a cause early prevents it from ever becoming a symptom.
Checkout error rate exceeding 2%, because it is a symptom directly tied to user-facing impact, whereas elevated database CPU may or may not ever translate into a real problem.
Both should page, since more coverage during an incident is always better than less.
Neither should page; both should be dashboard-only, since paging should be reserved exclusively for full outages.
assessments.explanation: Checkout error rate is a symptom-based signal -- it directly reflects what a real user is experiencing right now, which is exactly the kind of condition worth interrupting a human for. Database CPU at 60% is a cause-based signal that frequently doesn't correspond to any actual user-facing problem at all (a database can run comfortably at 60% CPU indefinitely); using it as a page trigger risks exactly the alert-fatigue pattern described earlier in this concept. Option A gets the direction backwards -- elevated CPU catching a 'cause early' sounds appealing but produces far more false-positive pages than genuine early warnings, since most CPU elevation never actually becomes a symptom. Option C ignores that indiscriminate paging degrades response quality for everything, including real incidents. Option D overcorrects -- symptom-based alerts like a real checkout error-rate spike are exactly what paging exists for, not something to demote to dashboard-only.

assessments.prompt: A new on-call rotation is being set up for a service that currently has a dozen CloudWatch alarms, most of them wired directly to page the on-call phone. Explain how you would redesign this into a paging strategy that avoids alert fatigue while still catching real incidents quickly.
assessments.modelAnswer: The starting point is auditing each of the existing alarms and classifying it as either symptom-based (does it directly reflect something a user or the business would notice -- elevated customer-facing error rate, degraded checkout latency, an availability drop on a critical endpoint) or cause-based (an internal condition, like CPU, memory, or queue depth, that may or may not ever produce a real symptom). Only symptom-based alarms should retain a direct paging action; every cause-based alarm should have its paging action removed and instead surface on a dashboard, or route to a lower-urgency ticket if it represents a trend worth investigating during business hours (disk usage climbing toward a limit weeks out, for instance) without needing to wake anyone up tonight. Where several related alarms tend to fire together for the same underlying incident -- elevated error rate, elevated latency, and a drop in healthy host count all spiking during the same outage -- a composite alarm combining them with AND/OR logic should replace the three individual pages with one, evaluated only when the combination genuinely indicates a real problem, while keeping each individual alarm visible on a dashboard for diagnosis. For any metric with genuine daily or weekly seasonality (traffic volume, request counts), a static threshold is likely to be either too loose to catch business-hours problems or too tight to survive normal overnight dips, so anomaly detection, which models the expected band of values as it naturally varies by time and day, is usually the better mechanism there. Finally, every alarm that does still page should have its alert text and any linked runbook reviewed for whether a person waking up to it at 3am has enough information to start diagnosing immediately, rather than first needing to reconstruct basic context about what the alarm even means. The overall goal isn't fewer alarms for their own sake -- it's making sure that when the on-call phone actually rings, it reliably means something that genuinely needs a human right now, which is precisely what keeps the team responding quickly instead of habitually dismissing pages.

concepts.title: Cost Optimization: Right-Sizing, Commitment Discounts, and Avoiding Bill Shock
concepts.description: AWS bills grow from a small number of well-understood patterns -- over-provisioned resources, the wrong pricing model for a workload's predictability, and things nobody remembered to turn off -- and a few concrete habits (utilization review, tagging, budgets, anomaly detection) catch most of the damage before an invoice does.
learningObjectives: Explain what right-sizing means and how to use real utilization data, rather than guesses, to identify over-provisioned resources.
Distinguish On-Demand, Savings Plans/Reserved capacity, and Spot pricing at an account-management level, and explain the risk of over-committing to reserved capacity.
Explain the classic 'forgot to turn it off' bill-shock pattern and identify the concrete resource types most commonly responsible for it.
Explain the role of resource tagging in cost allocation, and why untagged spend becomes a governance blind spot.
Design a basic cost-guardrail setup combining budgets, anomaly detection, and automated non-production shutdown schedules.

sections.heading: Right-Sizing: Using Real Utilization Data, Not Guesses
sections.body:
**Right-sizing** means matching a resource's provisioned capacity to what it actually uses, based on observed data rather than an initial guess made before anyone had real traffic or load to look at. It's extremely common, and understandable, for a team to over-provision at launch -- nobody wants to be the one who sized things too small and caused an outage, so 'a bit bigger than we think we need' becomes the default, and once something is running and working, revisiting that sizing decision later rarely feels urgent. The result, at scale across dozens or hundreds of resources, is a fleet quietly running well below the utilization it was sized for, with the difference between provisioned and actually-used capacity being pure waste, paid for every single hour.

The fix is mechanical rather than clever: pull actual CloudWatch utilization metrics (CPU, and memory via the CloudWatch agent, as covered in the earlier CloudWatch concept) over a representative window -- long enough to capture normal peak periods, not just a quiet afternoon -- and compare that to the instance's actual capacity. AWS's own **Compute Optimizer** does exactly this automatically across an entire account, analyzing historical utilization and recommending specific smaller (or, less commonly but just as importantly, larger, if something is under-provisioned and struggling) instance types, with an estimated savings or cost figure attached to each recommendation. Right-sizing isn't limited to EC2 either -- an RDS instance sized for a load spike that never materialized, or an EBS volume provisioned for far more IOPS than the workload ever calls for, are exactly the same pattern applied to different resource types, and the same discipline (look at real utilization, not the original provisioning guess) applies uniformly.

sections.heading: Commitment Discounts at Scale: Savings Plans and Reserved Capacity
sections.body:
At the level of a single instance, choosing between On-Demand, Savings Plans/Reserved Instances, and Spot is a workload-fit decision covered in depth elsewhere in this subject. At the level of an entire account or organization, the same choice becomes a portfolio decision, and it introduces a risk that doesn't show up when reasoning about just one instance: **over-commitment**. A Savings Plan or Reserved Instance purchase is a real financial commitment for a fixed term (1 or 3 years), sized against a forecast of steady-state usage -- and if actual usage later drops (a service gets decommissioned, a migration to a different instance family happens, a team scales down), the commitment doesn't shrink along with it. You keep paying for committed capacity you're no longer using, which is a different, and in some ways worse, flavor of waste than simple over-provisioning, because it's locked in for the remainder of the term rather than being something you can fix by resizing a single instance today.

The practical mitigation is twofold: track **coverage** (what fraction of actual usage is covered by a commitment, versus paying On-Demand rates for the uncovered remainder) and **utilization** (what fraction of the commitment you purchased is actually being used, versus paying for idle committed capacity) on an ongoing basis using Cost Explorer's dedicated Savings Plans/RI reports, not just at purchase time -- and to **ladder** commitments (staggering purchase terms and sizes over time) rather than making one large, all-at-once bet on a single forecast that may or may not hold up for the full 1-3 year term. Spot capacity remains a genuinely separate, complementary tool at this scale too: layering Spot underneath a Savings-Plan-covered baseline for variable, interruption-tolerant demand captures a steep discount on exactly the portion of usage that a fixed-term commitment would be the wrong shape for in the first place.

sections.heading: The Classic Bill-Shock Pattern: Forgot to Turn It Off
sections.body:
A large fraction of the most surprising, most avoidable AWS bills share the same root cause, phrased almost identically every time: something kept running, or kept existing, well after anyone needed it, and nobody was specifically watching for that. The pattern shows up in a handful of recurring, very concrete shapes. A **development or test environment** -- an EC2 fleet and an RDS instance -- provisioned to match production and left running 24/7, even though it's only ever used during a 9-to-6 weekday window; over a month, that's roughly 3.5x more running hours paid for than are ever actually used. An **unattached EBS volume**, left behind after its instance was terminated (EBS volumes are not automatically deleted with the instance unless explicitly configured to be), silently accruing storage cost indefinitely with nothing actively using it. An **Elastic IP address not associated with a running instance** -- AWS specifically charges for an idle, unassociated Elastic IP precisely to discourage squatting on a scarce IPv4 address without using it, which surprises people who assume a 'reserved but unused' resource should be free. **Orphaned EBS snapshots**, taken as routine backups and never cleaned up, accumulating for years past any realistic retention need. And a genuinely easy one to miss: a **NAT Gateway** left provisioned for a environment that's since been decommissioned in every other respect, still billing by the hour (and per-GB processed) for a resource nothing routes through anymore.

None of these require an engineer to do anything actively wrong or careless in the moment -- each one is the natural residue of infrastructure that was correctly created for a real purpose at the time, and correctly stopped being used, but never explicitly decommissioned. That's precisely what makes this pattern so persistent: it doesn't require a mistake so much as the simple absence of an explicit cleanup step, and cost, unlike most other kinds of technical debt, keeps compounding silently every single hour without anyone having to touch anything at all.

sections.heading: Tagging: Making Spend Attributable, Not Just Visible
sections.body:
None of the guardrails below work well without a basic prerequisite: knowing *whose* spend is *whose*. AWS's raw billing data groups cost by service and Region, but not, by default, by team, environment, or project -- that requires **cost allocation tags**, key/value pairs (like `Environment=dev`, `Team=payments`, `Project=checkout-redesign`) attached to resources at creation time and then activated in the Billing console so Cost Explorer and Cost and Usage Reports can group and filter by them. Untagged spend becomes a genuine governance blind spot: when a monthly bill shows an unexpected jump, the natural first question -- 'which team or project caused this' -- is unanswerable for any resource that was never tagged, forcing a slow, manual reconstruction from resource names, launch timestamps, and CloudTrail history instead of a straightforward Cost Explorer filter.

The practical fix is enforcing tagging at creation time rather than trying to retrofit it later -- via a tagging policy, an AWS Config rule that flags untagged resources, or a Service Control Policy that denies resource creation calls missing required tags entirely -- because tagging discipline that depends purely on everyone individually remembering to do it consistently tends to erode exactly when it matters most, during an incident or a rushed deployment. A small, consistently-enforced tag set (Environment, Team, Project, at minimum) turns 'why did the bill jump' from a forensic investigation into a two-minute Cost Explorer query, and is also precisely what makes it possible to answer 'is dev really costing as much as prod' -- a question that's otherwise surprisingly hard to answer with confidence.

sections.heading: Guardrails: Budgets, Anomaly Detection, and Scheduled Shutdowns Working Together
sections.body: Catching the patterns above before they show up as a surprise on next month's invoice takes a small, layered set of automated guardrails, each catching a slightly different failure shape. **AWS Budgets** lets you set a spending threshold (overall, or scoped to a specific tag, service, or account) and get notified -- or, with **budget actions**, automatically trigger a response, such as applying a restrictive IAM policy or stopping specific EC2/RDS instances -- when actual or forecasted spend crosses it; this is a blunt but effective backstop for 'are we broadly on track this month.' **Cost Anomaly Detection** is a complementary, finer-grained tool: rather than a fixed threshold, it uses machine learning to learn your normal day-to-day spend pattern per service or account and alerts on a statistically unusual deviation -- which is exactly what catches a sudden spend spike from, say, an accidentally-oversized instance launched in a test script, well before it accumulates enough to trip a monthly budget threshold at all. And for the specific, extremely common 'forgot to turn it off' pattern in non-production environments, the most direct fix is automation that doesn't rely on anyone remembering anything: a scheduled EventBridge rule invoking a small Lambda function (or AWS's own purpose-built Instance Scheduler solution) that stops tagged non-production instances outside business hours and starts them again each morning, converting a 24/7 cost into roughly a 9-to-6, weekdays-only one automatically, with no engineer needing to remember to shut anything down manually at the end of the day.

examples.title: A Nightly EventBridge Schedule That Stops Non-Production Instances Automatically
examples.explanation: This function is designed to be invoked by an EventBridge scheduled rule at 7pm on weekdays, filtering EC2 instances specifically by the `Environment=dev` or `Environment=test` tag and only among instances currently running, then stopping every match. A matching rule scheduled for 7am on weekdays would call `start_instances` on the same filtered set to bring them back for the workday. This directly targets the classic bill-shock pattern of a non-production environment left running 24/7 despite only being used roughly 9-to-6 on weekdays -- automating the shutdown removes the dependency on any engineer remembering to do it manually, which is precisely the gap that lets this specific pattern persist silently for months. Note this entire mechanism depends on the `Environment` tag actually being present and correct on every relevant instance -- an untagged dev instance would simply be invisible to this filter and would keep running 24/7 regardless.

examples.title: Finding Idle, Unattached, and Orphaned Resources With the CLI
examples.code:
# Unattached EBS volumes -- still billing for storage, attached to nothing
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query "Volumes[].{Id:VolumeId,SizeGiB:Size,Created:CreateTime}"

# Elastic IPs not associated with any running instance -- billed for being idle
aws ec2 describe-addresses \
  --query "Addresses[?AssociationId==null].{IP:PublicIp,AllocationId:AllocationId}"

# Snapshots older than 180 days -- candidates for review before assuming they're still needed
aws ec2 describe-snapshots --owner-ids self \
  --query "Snapshots[?StartTime<='2026-02-14'].{Id:SnapshotId,SizeGiB:VolumeSize,Created:StartTime}"
examples.explanation: None of these three queries look for anything actively broken -- they look for resources that are technically fine but have quietly stopped serving any purpose. The first finds EBS volumes in the `available` state, meaning they exist and are billing for storage but are not attached to any instance, which typically happens when an instance is terminated without explicitly deleting its non-root volumes. The second finds Elastic IPs with no `AssociationId`, meaning they aren't currently attached to a running instance or network interface -- AWS specifically charges an hourly rate for exactly this idle state, to discourage indefinitely holding scarce public IPv4 addresses without using them. The third lists snapshots older than a chosen cutoff, which doesn't mean they're safe to delete outright (some may be genuinely required for compliance retention), but flags them as candidates that deserve a deliberate keep-or-delete decision rather than existing purely by accident. Running queries like these periodically -- or better, automating them into a scheduled report -- is how the 'forgot to turn it off' pattern gets caught proactively instead of being discovered for the first time on an invoice.

examples.title: An AWS Budget With an Automatic Action, Not Just a Notification
examples.explanation: This budget is scoped specifically to spend tagged `Environment=dev` -- exactly the kind of tag-filtered scope that's only possible because those resources were tagged consistently in the first place, tying directly back to the tagging discussion in the explanation. Set at $500/month with a notification at 100% of that threshold, it's deliberately sized to catch the dev environment specifically ballooning to look like a second production environment, rather than being one broad, account-wide budget that couldn't distinguish 'dev costs spiked' from 'prod grew because the business grew, which is expected.' Beyond a plain notification like this one, AWS Budgets also supports budget actions that go further -- automatically applying a restrictive IAM policy to a target account, or stopping specific EC2/RDS instances, once a threshold is crossed -- turning a budget from a passive alert someone has to notice and act on into an active guardrail that intervenes on its own.

misconceptions.description: Once you've purchased Reserved Instances or a Savings Plan for your steady-state fleet, your infrastructure cost is now fixed and doesn't need further monitoring.
misconceptions.clarification: A commitment covers usage up to what was purchased -- if actual usage later exceeds it, the excess is billed at On-Demand rates on top of the commitment; if actual usage drops (a service shrinks, migrates to a different instance family, or gets decommissioned), you keep paying for the unused portion of the commitment for the remainder of its term regardless. Ongoing coverage and utilization tracking (via Cost Explorer's dedicated Savings Plans/RI reports) is necessary specifically because a commitment doesn't automatically resize itself to match changing real usage the way On-Demand billing does.

misconceptions.description: The AWS bill only grows when someone actively launches new resources, so if nobody is doing that, spend should stay flat.
misconceptions.clarification: A range of common resources continue accruing cost with zero active effort from anyone: an unattached EBS volume left behind after its instance was terminated, an Elastic IP not associated with a running instance, a NAT Gateway still provisioned for a decommissioned environment, and snapshots nobody ever revisits all keep billing indefinitely without any new resource being launched. This is precisely the 'forgot to turn it off' pattern -- spend growing, or simply failing to shrink, purely from the absence of an explicit cleanup step, not from any new deliberate action.

exercises.prompt: A monthly cost review shows the dev environment costing almost exactly as much as the production environment, even though the team only actively uses dev during roughly 45 out of the 168 hours in a week (9am-6pm, Monday-Friday). Diagnose why dev costs so much relative to its actual usage, and estimate the rough savings a fix would produce.
exercises.code:
environment  instance_hours_billed_per_month  monthly_cost
prod         2 x 730 hours = 1460               $290
dev          2 x 730 hours = 1460               $290
# dev is only actually used ~45 hours/week x ~4.3 weeks/month = ~194 hours/month
hints: Compare instance_hours_billed against actual usage hours for dev specifically -- what fraction of billed hours does 194 actual-use hours represent out of 1460 billed hours?
The instances themselves aren't necessarily oversized (that would be a right-sizing question) -- focus on whether they need to be running at all outside the hours anyone uses them.
Think about the specific automation from this concept's explanation that directly targets exactly this pattern -- running non-production infrastructure only during the hours it's actually used.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Automate a stop/start schedule for dev instances outside business hours,
# e.g. via an EventBridge rule + Lambda (see the earlier example), or AWS's
# Instance Scheduler solution, tagged Environment=dev

# Rough savings estimate:
# actual usage ~194 hours/month out of 1460 billed hours/month
# -> billing roughly 194/1460 = ~13% of current dev hours instead of 100%
# -> dev cost drops from ~$290/month toward roughly $290 * 0.13 ~= $38/month
# (ignoring any per-instance-hour minimums or non-compute costs that don't scale down)
exercises.solutionExplanation: Dev is billed for the exact same 1460 instance-hours per month as prod (2 instances running continuously, 730 hours each), despite only being genuinely used for roughly 194 of those hours -- about 13% of the billed time. This is the classic 24/7-for-a-9-to-6-workload pattern: nothing about the dev instances is necessarily oversized or misconfigured on a per-instance basis, they simply never stop running outside the hours anyone needs them. The fix is a scheduled automatic stop/start (an EventBridge-triggered Lambda, or AWS's Instance Scheduler) tagged to target exactly the dev environment, stopping instances each evening and starting them each morning on weekdays only. Since EC2 On-Demand billing is per-second while running and zero while stopped, cutting billed hours from 1460/month to roughly 194/month would be expected to cut dev's compute cost by a similar proportion -- from roughly $290/month toward something closer to $38/month, a meaningful, fully automatic saving that required no change to the instances themselves, only to when they're allowed to run.

exercises.prompt: Write a boto3 (Python) script that finds every EBS volume in the 'available' (unattached) state across the account and prints its volume ID, size, and age in days, so a team can review them before deciding what to delete.
hints: describe_volumes accepts a Filters argument -- filter on Name='status', Values=['available'] to get only unattached volumes.
Each volume dict in the response includes 'VolumeId', 'Size' (GiB), and 'CreateTime' (a timezone-aware datetime).
Subtract CreateTime from the current UTC time (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) to get a timedelta, then use .days for a whole-number age.
exercises.solutionCode:
import boto3
from datetime import datetime, timezone

ec2 = boto3.client("ec2")

def find_unattached_volumes():
    response = ec2.describe_volumes(
        Filters=[{"Name": "status", "Values": ["available"]}]
    )
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    for volume in response["Volumes"]:
        age_days = (now - volume["CreateTime"]).days
        print(f"{volume['VolumeId']}  {volume['Size']}GiB  age={age_days}d")

find_unattached_volumes()
exercises.solutionExplanation: The `Filters=[{"Name": "status", "Values": ["available"]}]` argument restricts `describe_volumes` to only volumes in the `available` state, which specifically means they exist and are billing for storage but are not currently attached to any instance -- exactly the unattached-volume waste pattern from the explanation. For each matching volume, `volume["Size"]` gives its provisioned size in GiB (which is what determines its storage cost) and subtracting `volume["CreateTime"]` from the current UTC time gives a `timedelta`, whose `.days` attribute is a simple whole-number age in days -- useful context for a team deciding whether a volume that's been sitting unattached for 400 days is obviously safe to delete versus one from yesterday that might still be mid-migration. This script deliberately only reports candidates rather than deleting anything automatically, since an unattached volume isn't necessarily safe to delete without a human confirming it -- automating discovery while keeping the actual deletion decision manual is a reasonable, conservative default for this kind of cleanup.

assessments.prompt: A finance team notices AWS spend jumped noticeably last Tuesday, in a way that's still comfortably under the monthly budget threshold everyone monitors. Which tool is specifically designed to catch a spike like this quickly, rather than waiting for it to accumulate into a budget breach?
options: AWS Budgets, since it tracks monthly spend against a threshold.
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, since it learns normal day-to-day spend patterns and flags statistically unusual deviations, independent of any fixed monthly threshold.
Resource tagging, since it makes spend attributable to a specific team or project.
Savings Plans coverage reports, since they show how much of current usage is covered by a commitment.
assessments.explanation: The scenario describes a real, sudden day-level spike that hasn't yet accumulated enough to breach a monthly budget -- exactly the gap AWS Budgets (option A) is poorly suited to catch quickly, since it's fundamentally a threshold-over-a-period tool, not a day-to-day pattern-deviation detector. Cost Anomaly Detection is purpose-built for precisely this case: it models expected day-to-day spend and alerts on a statistically unusual deviation as soon as it happens, regardless of whether the monthly total is anywhere near a budget limit yet. Tagging (option C) helps attribute spend once you're investigating, but doesn't itself detect or flag anything unusual. Savings Plans coverage reports (option D) are about commitment utilization, unrelated to detecting an unexpected spend spike.

assessments.prompt: A colleague says: 'We should just pick the biggest, most reserved-capacity-covered instances everywhere -- bigger is safer, and reserved is cheaper.' Explain what's wrong with applying this as a blanket rule, and describe the actual reasoning process you'd use instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Both halves of that rule skip the step that actually determines whether they help: looking at real usage data. 'Bigger is safer' assumes more capacity can only be a good thing, but an oversized instance running at 15% CPU utilization isn't safer than a correctly-sized one at 60-70% -- it's simply paying for headroom that's never used, with no corresponding reliability benefit, since a correctly-sized instance with reasonable utilization is not meaningfully more failure-prone than an oversized one. Right-sizing based on actual CloudWatch utilization data (and tools like Compute Optimizer that automate exactly this analysis) is how you find the genuine mismatch between provisioned and used capacity, rather than assuming bigger is a free safety margin. 'Reserved is cheaper' is true only for usage that's genuinely steady-state and predictable for the length of the commitment term -- applying it blanket-wide, including to workloads still being validated or ones with genuinely variable demand, risks over-committing: paying for reserved capacity that later goes unused because the workload shrank, moved to a different instance family, or turned out not to need that much capacity after all, with no way to get out of the remaining commitment term. The better process is to separate the two decisions and apply real data to each: first, right-size based on actual observed utilization, choosing an instance family and size that matches the genuine bottleneck (CPU, memory, or otherwise) rather than defaulting to bigger; second, and only for the resulting right-sized footprint, apply a pricing model matched to that specific workload's predictability -- Reserved/Savings Plans for the portion that's demonstrably steady-state and long-lived, On-Demand for anything still being validated or genuinely variable, and Spot for anything stateless and interruption-tolerant. Treating 'bigger' and 'reserved' as universal defaults skips exactly the analysis that would tell you whether either one is actually buying anything in a given case.
